title: Singapore Pays People to Read
paragraphs: Many people today spend hours scrolling through social media on their phones but rarely sit down with a book. In Singapore, the government has come up with an unusual solution: paying people to read.

The National Library Board (NLB), which runs Singapore's public libraries, launched a national reading campaign called ReadSG on September 6, 2026. As part of the campaign, a pilot program called the ReadSG Challenge is running until December 31, 2026.

The goal of the challenge is to encourage people to read for at least 15 minutes a day. Participants sign up on a government platform called CrowdTask SG and record their reading sessions once a day. The system works on an honor basis, which means participants report their own reading. Each qualifying session earns 20 virtual coins, which can be exchanged for cash value and spent at participating businesses.

However, nobody is going to get rich from reading. A total of 1,000 coins is worth just 1 Singapore dollar, so it takes 50 days of reading to earn that amount. The small reward is deliberate. The program is designed to gently encourage people to build a reading habit, rather than to make money.

Melissa Tam, the chief executive of the NLB, explained that people today live in a world with an extraordinary amount of content, information and stimulation, which may lead them to engage less deeply with what they read. Since habits form through small, regular actions, the campaign begins with a simple goal: just read for 15 minutes a day.

Singapore already has high levels of reading. According to reports, 89% of adults read more than once a week. But only 28% said they read books. Experts point out that while people still read words on screens, the kind of deep reading that requires long periods of attention may be happening less often.
The scheme has attracted international attention, including from CNN and The Guardian. However, some commentators have asked whether people will continue reading once the rewards stop.
